label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.quote: every member that existed but the researcher woke at its own minute
findings.why: A busy first reader meets 'wake', 'member' and 'own minute' as if known, and has to stop and decode the opening paragraph.
It directs the reader to a figure instead of letting the sentence carry the point.

findings.quote: That is the lesson the register draws: redaction does not reach a commit already pushed.
findings.why: The narrator reports what the register says with no 'I' and no hindsight, where the editor could say what he took from it.

findings.quote: The argument is in the wake record, both halves of it
findings.why: It restates the scene the reader has just read, and reports it rather than speaking as the editor.

findings.quote: Same kind of mistake. Found before the close this time, and redacted in the same wake.
findings.why: The narrator has just said this in the previous paragraph, so the researcher's line tells the same thing twice.

findings.quote: six agents, a clock and a brake
findings.why: 'Brake' is not yet pinned down as the hold for a reader arriving at this chapter, and the Wardley map arrives only afterwards.

findings.quote: answers on the live slides, the new pieces into the deck, the team's own policies into the talk
findings.why: A list of insider shorthand with no example; a team member cannot picture what one instruction looked like or copy it.

findings.quote: It is a small scene, and it is the whole of my talk in miniature.
findings.why: The scene is told, then explained, then Studio's answer is repeated in a third form; the takeaway survives with one of them.

findings.quote: Part one was final and not yet locked. The lock tool existed. One session was open
findings.why: A run of short sentences where one running sentence would carry the thought and the forward references.

findings.quote: Giving one small thing to somebody today, and changing it from what they say
findings.why: The try-this card is abstract; a team member wants a concrete first action with their own agent, not a feeling that 'it starts to feel different'.

findings.quote: Add a second agent only when the first is busy.
findings.why: My case is a team where each person already has an agent; the steps only half answer who holds the shared brief, the board and the hold, and 'who may lift the hold when its owner is away' is left as advice.

findings.quote: the ones Start here gave you as a formula
findings.why: Points back to a page the reader may not have read, so the steps lean on memory instead of standing alone.

findings.quote: A brief and rules in plain words. A check every change passes. A hold anyone can pull
findings.why: Seven short sentences in a row, a triad-style list that reads as a slogan rather than the thought running.

findings.quote: But build it the same way, and then do it again.
findings.why: The bold line two lines later says the same thing again.

what_holds: 08-hours-four-and-five-before-dawn.md: the two failures, each with a one-line rule (the branch wins), and the closing Something to try about where 'done' is measured is a copyable check.
15-hour-eighteen-faster-than-the-clock.md: the brakes held under pressure, and Studio refusing a relayed word, give a concrete pattern a team could adopt.

23-principles-and-build-your-own.md: the five steps with what to do and what to check, the shop owner and newsroom examples, and the tear-out checklist are the most directly copyable part of the book.
notes: As a team member I would start tomorrow with step 2 (a page of rules with a stop line). What I would still need is how several people share one brief, one board and one hold, each with their own agent; the chapters mostly tell one editor's day and so lean on one central person, which is a deal-breaker unless chapter 23 answers it more fully.
